overview: Apache is a broad name for distinct Indigenous peoples and communities, not a single kingdom with one capital or ruler. Their histories include homelands in the Southwest and northern Mexico, forced removals and continuing tribal governments. The examples here identify particular communities so that one group’s experience is not mistaken for everyone’s.

periods.title: Mescalero confinement at Bosque Redondo
periods.summary: U.S. forces removed Mescalero people from their homelands in late 1862 and early 1863. Many escaped Bosque Redondo in November 1865 and returned toward the mountains.

periods.title: A reservation at Mescalero
periods.summary: An executive order of 29 May 1873 established the Mescalero reservation. This was a change in land administration, not the beginning of the people’s history.

periods.title: Chiricahua and Warm Springs imprisonment
periods.summary: The ancestors of the Fort Sill Apache endured forced displacement and prisoner-of-war status. After detention in Florida and Alabama, they were moved to Fort Sill in 1894.

periods.title: Different paths out of captivity
periods.summary: Some Chiricahua families moved to Mescalero in 1913. Others remained in Oklahoma, where release and allotments followed in 1914. These communities developed distinct institutional histories.

periods.title: Mildred Cleghorn leads at Fort Sill
periods.summary: Teacher and doll maker Mildred Imach Cleghorn became chairperson of the newly organized Fort Sill Apache government, bringing cultural preservation into her public leadership.

periods.title: Fort Apache firefighting recognition
periods.summary: The Fort Apache crew became the first fully certified Native American Interagency Hotshot Crew, according to the Bureau of Indian Affairs.

periods.title: San Carlos administers the Geronimo crew
periods.summary: The San Carlos Apache Tribal Natural Resources Program began managing the fully certified Geronimo Interagency Hotshot Crew, linking specialized firefighting with tribal administration.

sections.title: Food, shelter and knowledge of place

items.text: Mescalero history describes short, rounded brush shelters and hide-covered tipis suited to temporary camps. Hunting and gathering supplied meat, berries, nuts, roots and other foods. Agave hearts were especially important. These descriptions concern Mescalero practice and should not be treated as the complete diet or housing pattern of every Apache community.

At Guadalupe Mountains, tribal participants harvested agave and attempted a pit roast described by Mescalero preservation officer Holly Houghten. The soil failed to retain enough heat. Her account shows that successful roasting depends on practical knowledge of a particular place, not simply on identifying a plant or copying a pit’s shape.

Houghten also explains why springs, plants, animals and routes matter alongside excavated sites. A traditional-use plant book, supported by White Sands Missile Range, helped connect heritage protection with teaching younger community members. Harvesting and visits to the landscape supplied knowledge that a list of archaeological objects alone could not provide.

At Canyon Day, the White Mountain Apache People’s Farm combines food production with education. A FoodCorps participant describes selling produce locally and helping children learn where food comes from and how to grow it. This is a particular community initiative linking agriculture, household food and cultural knowledge.

A Chiricahua water vessel in the National Museum of the American Indian combines twined plant fiber, a hide thong and a pitch coating. Its catalogue dates it to 1880 to 1909 and records collection from Martin Keta at Fort Sill in 1909. It preserves evidence of a light woven container adapted to holding water during the community’s period of imprisonment.

A Jicarilla Apache basket in the same museum was made with coiled, dyed sumac. The catalogue gives a production range of 1890 to 1915 and records acquisition in 1916 from an earlier collection. Its maker and earlier history are unknown, so its materials and technique are better documented than its precise household use.

San Carlos Apache musician Chesley Wilson described making a short, single-string violin from an agave stalk. In his oral-history transcript, instrument making sits beside memories of singing and performing with his father. The account connects a locally available plant with musical skill and learning within a family.

Wilson also recalled being taught to navigate by stars and gather acorns and agave as a child. His testimony places songs, language and practical knowledge within the same process of growing up. It is his remembered experience, rather than a claim that every child received identical instruction.

Mildred Imach Cleghorn made dolls with clothing representing many Native peoples she encountered through teaching. Born a prisoner of war in 1910, she later taught home economics and kindergarten and became a cultural and political leader. Her work shows artistic achievement extending through education and public service.

The U.S. military forced Mescalero people to Bosque Redondo in 1862 and 1863. The National Park Service’s historical study records their escape on 3 November 1865, followed by movement toward the Guadalupe and Sacramento mountains. A later reservation date cannot summarize this experience of coercion, resistance and return.

The Fort Sill Apache trace their community to Chiricahua and Warm Springs ancestors held by the United States from 1886 to 1914. Their history includes confinement far from their Southwest homelands and settlement in Oklahoma after release. The end of armed resistance did not mean that Apache people or their institutions ceased to exist.

The move to Fort Sill in 1894 did not deliver a secure permanent homeland. Later pressure to leave divided families’ choices: some accepted relocation to Mescalero, while others insisted on remaining in Oklahoma. The tribe’s account describes negotiations over land as part of the struggle to leave prisoner-of-war status.

The Fort Apache Interagency Hotshot Crew achieved full certification in 1982. Such crews undertake demanding wildland fire work, including building fire lines and coordinating with aircraft and engines. This achievement belongs to an organized workforce with specialized training, not to an assumption that environmental knowledge is automatic or identical among all Apache people.

The Geronimo crew is a separate organization administered by the San Carlos Apache Tribe since 1996, with Bureau of Indian Affairs sponsorship for interagency standards. Its history is an example of tribal management of a professional public-safety service, alongside employment and technical training.

ending.text: Apache peoples continue through distinct communities and tribal governments. Forced confinement, loss of land and restrictions on movement changed their political circumstances. There was no single fall of an Apache kingdom, and the imported map entry’s endpoint in 1650 does not mark their disappearance.
